name: Multimodal Embeddings
question: Can one search cover text, images and more?
summary: Multimodal models embed different kinds of content into one shared vector space, so a text query can find an image and an image can find related text. CLIP-style models learn this by aligning millions of images with their captions.
useCases: Product catalogues searched by description or photo
Slides, scanned pages and documents full of charts
Media libraries: photos, video frames, audio

items.detail: text and images compared with the same cosine similarity
text → image, image → text, image → image
embed page screenshots to keep tables and charts (e.g. ColPali)

steps: Pick a model that covers your media types and languages
Embed images (or page renders) and text into the same index
Store a link to the original asset and any extracted text as metadata
Test cross-modal queries in both directions with real examples
pitfalls: Fine visual detail such as small text or exact counts is often lost
Larger vectors and more storage per item
Quality varies a lot by domain, e.g. medical images or engineering drawings
caption: Squares are images, the circle is the text query. It lands beside the matching photos.

steps.title: Pick a model that covers both media
steps.text: A CLIP-style model has an image encoder and a text encoder trained together, so both produce vectors in one space.

steps.title: Embed the catalogue photos
steps.text: Each product photo becomes one vector. A red shoe whose seller wrote only “New arrival, SKU 4471” is still findable by what it looks like.

steps.title: Embed the text query
steps.text: “red running shoe” goes through the text encoder and lands in the same space as the photos.

steps.title: Compare across media
steps.text: Cosine similarity works as usual. Scores of 0.31 and 0.29 look low, but text–image scores are low in general: the ranking is what counts.

steps.title: Search by photo too
steps.text: A customer’s photo goes through the image encoder and lands next to the same two red shoes: image-to-image search, same index.

steps.title: Store links and test both directions
steps.text: Keep each asset’s URL and caption as metadata, then test text-to-image and image-to-image queries on real examples.

pros: Search images by description and by example photo
Finds items whose text metadata is poor or missing
One index and one similarity for several media
Page-image models keep tables and charts in documents
cons: Fine visual detail such as small printed text is often lost
Text–image scores are low and model-specific, so thresholds are tricky
More storage: one or more vectors per asset
Quality varies a lot by domain
avoidWhen: All content is plain text (a text model is cheaper and stronger)
The answer depends on exact small text in images (use OCR as well)

One red running shoe has a useless seller description; another shoe has a tiny AIR print on its heel. Choose the model and what to index so every query finds its products.

Choose a text-only embedding model or a CLIP-style multimodal model.
Tick what gets indexed: product descriptions, product photos, or both.

goals: Explain how a shared vector space lets text find images and images find text
Explain why text–image scores are low and why ranking matters more than thresholds
Name what image embeddings miss and how to cover it

practice.scenario: A shopping app lets users type “red running shoe with white sole” or upload a photo. Product images and descriptions sit in one CLIP index, so both kinds of query return the same shoes.

industries.use: Search by photo or by description
Match damage photos to similar past claims
Search slide decks and scanned forms by what they show

practice.analogy: A bilingual guide who understands a description and a photo equally well, and points to the same shelf for both.

library.name: CLIP via sentence-transformers
library.what: Loads CLIP models with the same encode() call used for text, so images and text land in one space.

samples.code:
from PIL import Image
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")          # text and images, one space
paths = ["shoe_red.jpg", "shoe_blue.jpg", "handbag.jpg"]
img_vecs = model.encode([Image.open(p) for p in paths])

query = model.encode("red running shoe with white sole")
best = util.cos_sim(query, img_vecs)[0].argmax()
print(paths[int(best)])                               # shoe_red.jpg

# image -> image works the same way:
# model.encode(Image.open("customer_photo.jpg"))

numericDrill.question: With a CLIP model, a text query scores 0.31, 0.12 and 0.29 against three images. Image 1 is the right match. Why are the scores so low, and what matters?
numericDrill.answer: Text–image similarities in CLIP-style models are usually low in absolute terms. What matters is the ranking: image 1 comes first. Tune any threshold per model on your own data.

interview.question: How does CLIP put text and images in one space?
interview.answer: It trains an image encoder and a text encoder together with a contrastive loss on image–caption pairs, pulling matching pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart.

interview.question: How would you search scanned PDFs full of charts and tables?
interview.answer: Either OCR and layout parsing into text chunks, or embed page images directly with a document-image model such as ColPali, which keeps the visual layout. Many systems combine both.

mistakes.fix: Tune thresholds per model on your data

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the link to the original asset
mistakes.fix: Store the asset URL and extracted text as metadata

quiz.question: Customers upload photos of broken parts to find the right spare. Which technique fits?
quiz.explanation: Photos and product listings need to share one vector space.

quiz.question: An insurer wants to find past claims whose damage photos look like a new one. How?
options: Embed claim photos with an image encoder and search image-to-image
Ask an LLM to describe the photo and search for the exact caption
quiz.explanation: Image-to-image search compares photo vectors directly in the same space.

quiz.question: Which statements about CLIP-style models are true? Select all that apply.
options: The image and text encoders are trained together
In the original CLIP models, matching text–image cosine scores are typically low, around 0.2 to 0.35
They read small serial numbers reliably
quiz.explanation: CLIP aligns images and captions; its scores are low in absolute terms, and fine printed detail is a known weakness.

quiz.question: A 0.8 similarity threshold copied from text search returns no products for text-to-image queries. What do you do?
options: Rank and keep the top k, or tune a threshold for this model
quiz.explanation: Cross-modal scores are low for everyone. The ranking is what carries the signal.

quiz.question: A bank must search thousands of scanned KYC forms full of tables and stamps. Which approach fits?
options: OCR and layout parsing, or page-image retrieval such as ColPali
A text-only model on the file names
quiz.explanation: Either extract the text or embed the page images; many systems combine both.

quiz.question: 2 million images are embedded at 512 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the vectors need?
A red running shoe is listed as “New arrival, SKU 4471”, and text search never shows it for “red running shoe”. What fixes this?
options: Index product photos with a multimodal model
quiz.explanation: Its photo carries what the description lacks.

quiz.question: Which are real risks when using general image embeddings on patient photos? Select all that apply.
options: Clinical images differ from web photos, so quality can drop
Embedding patient photos brings privacy and consent obligations
General models always beat specialist ones
quiz.explanation: Domain shift, lost detail and data protection are the main concerns; specialist models often do better.

quiz.question: Buyers type “sunny balcony with plants” to search listing photos. What kind of search is this?
options: Text-to-image search in a shared space
quiz.explanation: The text encoder embeds the query; it is compared with photo vectors.

quiz.question: Students search lecture slides where the answer is in a diagram with a short caption. What fits best?
options: A model that embeds slide images or mixed text and images
A text model on file names
quiz.explanation: Slides carry meaning in their visuals, so embed the rendered slide, not just its text.

quiz.question: Text-to-text and text-to-image scores are merged by raw value, and photo matches never appear. Why?
options: Text–text scores sit on a higher scale, so they always win
Photos cannot be searched with text
Cosine similarity is undefined for images
quiz.explanation: Normalize each list or merge by rank, for example with reciprocal rank fusion.

quiz.question: Shoppers search one catalogue in Hindi, Tamil and English, by text or photo. What should you look for?
options: A multilingual multimodal model, with a licence that allows commercial use
quiz.explanation: Language coverage and licence both matter; some open multilingual weights are non-commercial.

quiz.question: What should each image vector’s metadata include? Select all that apply.
options: The URL of the original image
quiz.explanation: Metadata links results back to products and enables filtering. Pixels belong in object storage.

quiz.question: Engineers search drawings by exact part numbers printed on them. What should you add to image embeddings?
options: OCR the drawings and index the text with BM25
quiz.explanation: Image embeddings lose small printed text; OCR plus keyword search catches exact numbers.

quiz.question: A 2-hour video is sampled at one frame every 2 seconds for embedding. How many frames is that?
quiz.explanation: 7,200 seconds ÷ 2 = 3,600 frames, each linked to its timestamp.

quiz.question: Photos were embedded with a CLIP image encoder, but queries use a separate sentence-transformers text model. What happens?
options: Scores are meaningless, because the vectors come from unrelated spaces
It works if the dimensions match
Results improve because the text model is stronger
quiz.explanation: Only the paired text encoder produces vectors in the image encoder’s space.

quiz.question: Which checks belong in a multimodal search evaluation? Select all that apply.
options: Fine-detail queries, to confirm text indexing covers them
Only checking that the average cosine is above 0.5
quiz.explanation: Test each direction and the known weak spot. Average scores say nothing about ranking quality.

quiz.question: Which of these are cross-modal searches? Select all that apply.
options: A text query that retrieves product photos
A photo that retrieves a manual page
A text question that retrieves a text FAQ
A photo of router lights that retrieves a troubleshooting article
quiz.explanation: Cross-modal means the query and result are different media.

quiz.question: A general CLIP model ranks dermatology photos poorly. What is the most promising next step?
options: Fine-tune on labelled domain image–text pairs, or use a domain-specific model
Convert the photos to binary vectors
quiz.explanation: Domain shift is fixed with domain data, often through contrastive fine-tuning.

quiz.question: How does SigLIP’s training differ from the original CLIP?
options: It uses a pairwise sigmoid loss instead of a softmax over the batch
It uses BM25 scores as labels
quiz.explanation: SigLIP scores each image–text pair independently with a sigmoid loss.
